newsitem.title: UK: Soccer-Newcastle to press ahead with flotation.
newsitem.headline: Soccer-Newcastle to press ahead with flotation.

text.p: English premier league soccer club Newcastle United vowed on Thursday to press ahead with a stock market flotation despite the shock resignation of manager Kevin Keegan 24 hours earlier.

"This doesn't alter the float timetable," a club spokesman said. Newcastle last month confirmed plans to join the London Stock Exchange this spring and said further details of the listing would be made available in mid-January.
A further announcement is expected next week on the flotation of the club owned by property magnate Sir John Hall. Analysts say it is likely to be valued at over 150 million pounds ($255 million).

The spokesman denied a newspaper report that merchant bank Natwest Markets had forced the hand of the former England captain, whose departure plunged the soccer-mad northern city of Newcastle into the depths of despair.
A report in The Times on Thursday said that Natwest, which is handling the flotation, had told Keegan that he must resign immediately if he was serious about alleged threats to quit.
The report said that Natwest did not want Keegan to walk out on the club while it was marketing Newcastle shares.

The spokesman also dismissed a suggestion by The Times that chairman Hall, who has pumped millions of pounds into the club, would step down when the soccer side was floated. The report said he intended to focus on other parts of the Newcastle sporting empire such as the rugby union club.
Newcastle, still in contention for the English premier league title and the F.A. and UEFA Cups, were rocked on Wednesday by Keegan's abrupt departure.
Keegan joined Newcastle five years ago when the club was languishing near the foot of the old second division but his drive and Hall's money have restored the team's fortunes.

The club now boast stars such as England striker Alan Shearer, signed for a world record 15 million pounds last year, plus foreign talents including Frenchman David Ginola and Colombian Faustino Asprilla.
The 36,000 seats at its St. James' Park stadium are always sold out and the club plans a new 65 million pound ($110 million) stadium, with a capacity of 55,000, to meet the demand.
Share analysts said that the departure of Keegan from the club's management could unsettle potential investors but the damage could be repaired by the swift appointment of a high-profile replacement.

An increasing number of British soccer clubs have sought stock market listings to raise funds and widen ownership. The large sums of money flowing into the game through a television deal with Rupert Murdoch-controlled satellite broadcaster BSkyB have made the issues popular with investors.

The appetite for soccer stocks is illustrated by Newcastle's less glamorous northeast neighbours Sunderland, one of the lesser lights of the premier league. Shares in Sunderland have soared from 585 to 707.5 pence in just two weeks of trading.
